title: Nansen and Johansen Winter in a Stone Hut
text:
In March 1895 Fridtjof Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left their ship Fram, which was drifting with the Arctic ice, and set out with dogs, sledges and kayaks to try for the North Pole. On 8 April they reached 86 degrees 14 minutes north, farther north than anyone before them, then turned back toward land.

The retreat took months. By late August they reached a barren island in Franz Josef Land, too late in the year to go on. They built a hut of stones and moss, roofed with walrus hides, barely big enough for two men lying down, and settled in for the polar night. They lived on walrus and polar bear meat, burned blubber for heat and light, and wore the same greasy clothes for nine months.

Nansen was a famous scientist and the expedition leader; Johansen was a reserve army officer. In Farthest North Nansen writes that through all of this they had continued to address each other with the formal Norwegian "De". On New Year's Eve, in their filthy hut, Nansen proposed that they drop it and use the familiar "du". They lived side by side through the whole winter without a serious quarrel.

In May 1896 they set off south again. In June, by pure chance, Nansen met the British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora, whose expedition took them home. Fram arrived in Norway a week after them.
lesson: Two people sharing hardship in a small space need patience and respect more than skill. Courtesy and small gestures keep a partnership intact through long strain.
location: Jackson Island, Franz Josef Land (modern Russia)
